title: GOD CALLED HIS NAME… BUT ALMOST NOBODY REMEMBERS HIM: THE FORGOTTEN CRAFTSMAN WHO HELPED BUILD A PLACE FOR GOD'S GLORY
paragraphs: GOD CALLED HIS NAME… BUT ALMOST NOBODY REMEMBERS HIM: THE FORGOTTEN CRAFTSMAN WHO HELPED BUILD A PLACE FOR GOD'S GLORY

His name was Oholiab. He wasn't Moses. He wasn't Aaron. He wasn't even the first craftsman mentioned. Yet God personally chose him for a sacred assignment—and his story carries a powerful message for everyone who has ever felt overlooked, underestimated, or invisible while trying to serve the Lord.
There is a particular kind of pain that comes from giving your best and wondering whether anybody notices.
You show up. You serve. You sacrifice. You stay when others leave.
You do the work nobody celebrates.

You pray for people who never know you prayed. You help behind the scenes while someone else receives the applause. You pour your heart into something meaningful, only to watch another person's name become associated with its success.
And somewhere, deep inside, a question begins to form.
Lord, do You even see me?
Perhaps you have never said those words aloud.
Perhaps you feel guilty for even thinking them.
After all, you are supposed to serve God without seeking recognition. You know that. You believe that.
But knowing the right thing doesn't automatically silence the ache of being overlooked.
And that is where a man named Oholiab enters the story.
Not from a palace.
Not from a battlefield.
Not from a pulpit.
But from a workshop.

And if you have ever felt that your contribution was too small, your position too ordinary, or your name too insignificant to matter in the kingdom of God, you need to know what Scripture actually says about this man.
Because tucked inside the book of Exodus is a truth that can change the way you see your work, your gifts, and your place in God's purposes.
God does not need the world to recognize your name before He can call you by it.
And Oholiab is living proof.
In Exodus 31, the Israelites were still in the wilderness. God had delivered them from Egypt, brought them through the sea, and established His covenant with them at Sinai.
Now He was giving Moses detailed instructions for the tabernacle—the sacred dwelling place that would stand at the center of Israel's worship.
This was not simply a beautiful tent.
It was the place where God's presence would be manifested among His covenant people.
Every curtain mattered.
Every furnishing mattered.
Every measurement, material, and design carried significance within the pattern God revealed to Moses.
The work required extraordinary craftsmanship.
And God did something remarkable.
He named the workers.

Exodus 31:2–5 identifies Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah. God declared that He had filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God, giving him wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and skill for artistic work.
Then comes verse 6.
A verse many believers have read without stopping long enough to feel its weight.
The King James Version records God's words:
“And I, behold, I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.” — Exodus 31:6
Aholiab is the traditional spelling used in the King James Version. Many modern English translations render his name Oholiab.
Now notice something.
God did not merely say, “Find someone to help Bezalel.”
He identified the man.
His name.
His father.
His tribe.
Before Oholiab's work became visible to the nation, his identity was already known to God.
And there is something profoundly comforting about that.
The God who commanded the construction of a sanctuary did not overlook the individual craftsman who would help build it.
The One who governed the covenant, the worship, and the destiny of Israel also knew the name of a worker whose hands would shape sacred materials.
Maybe you needed to remember that tonight.
Because you may feel like a supporting character in everybody else's story.
But you are not invisible to the Lord.
The original Hebrew makes this passage even more meaningful.
Exodus 31:6 begins:
וַאֲנִי הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי אִתּוֹ אֵת אָהֳלִיאָב
Va'ani hinneh natatti itto et Oholiav.
A close rendering is:
“And I, behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab.”
The Hebrew verb נָתַתִּי (natatti) literally means “I have given.” In this context, it communicates God's provision or appointment of Oholiab alongside Bezalel.
The expression אִתּוֹ (itto) means “with him.”
That small phrase matters.
Oholiab was appointed with Bezalel.
Not as a rival.
Not as an accidental replacement.
Not as someone whose value depended on becoming more famous than the man beside him.
God appointed them to participate in the same sacred work.
And there is a lesson here that the modern church desperately needs.
You do not have to compete with someone else's calling to be faithful to your own.
Bezalel had his assignment.
Oholiab had his assignment.
Both were needed for the work God commanded.
We live in a world that constantly teaches people to measure their importance by visibility.
Followers.
Recognition.
Influence.
Titles.
Applause.
And sometimes that thinking quietly enters the church.
The person holding the microphone seems more important than the person preparing the room.
The preacher seems more valuable than the volunteer.
The public testimony receives attention while the private obedience goes unnoticed.
But Exodus 31 confronts that way of thinking.
God's sacred work required more than one person.
And He Himself appointed the people who would carry it out.
Perhaps the most painful part of being overlooked is not that others fail to recognize you.
It is that, eventually, you begin to question whether your work matters at all.
You start comparing your gifts with someone else's.
You see their opportunities and wonder why yours are different.
You watch another person flourish in a visible ministry while your own responsibilities seem repetitive and ordinary.
And if you are not careful, comparison begins poisoning something that once brought you joy.
You stop asking, “Lord, how can I serve You faithfully?”
And start asking, “Lord, why am I not where they are?”
Oholiab's story invites us to ask a better question.
What if faithfulness matters more than fame?
But we must go deeper.
Because Oholiab was not simply an anonymous assistant.
Scripture tells us more about him than many people realize.
In Exodus 35:34, Moses explains that God had given Bezalel and Oholiab the ability to teach others.
Then Exodus 35:35 describes their God-given skill in craftsmanship, design, embroidery, and weaving.
Oholiab was not merely carrying supplies while Bezalel did the important work.
He possessed real ability.
He was involved in skilled craftsmanship.
And he was entrusted with helping others learn.
That is a beautiful detail.
Because God did not merely provide workers capable of making something.
He provided workers capable of passing knowledge on.
Think about that.
Some people are gifted at creating.
Others are gifted at teaching.
Some are able to do both.
And the ability to strengthen another person's hands can be just as meaningful as the ability to produce something with your own.
A gifted person can accomplish valuable work.
A gifted person who teaches others can help multiply that work.
Oholiab's contribution was not insignificant simply because Bezalel was named first.
And this brings us to a truth that can challenge the way we think about spiritual calling.
Not every God-given assignment looks religious from the outside.
Oholiab was a craftsman.
He worked with materials.
He understood patterns, colors, and construction.
His service involved practical skills.
And those skills became part of the worship life of Israel.
The passage does not teach that every profession automatically becomes holy simply because someone is talented.
It teaches something more precise and powerful: God deliberately equipped and appointed skilled people for the work He commanded.
Their craftsmanship was not a distraction from obedience.
It was part of their obedience.
And that should make us reconsider how casually we sometimes dismiss ordinary labor.
The carpenter who works honestly.
The mother who patiently teaches her children.
The father who provides faithfully without recognition.
The teacher who helps a struggling student understand.
The writer who labors over words that may encourage someone toward the truth.
The artist who uses creativity with integrity.
The believer who quietly repairs, organizes, cooks, cleans, gives, and serves.
These are not all equivalent to Oholiab's unique appointment to build the tabernacle. Scripture does not promise every occupation the same role in redemptive history.
But his story reminds us that practical skill is not beneath God's concern.
And the New Testament gives Christians a clear principle for ordinary work.
Colossians 3:23–24 teaches believers to work heartily for the Lord rather than merely for human approval, remembering that they ultimately serve Christ.
That changes things.
Because suddenly the question is not merely whether someone applauds what you have done.
The question becomes whether your work is offered with faithfulness before the Lord.
And sometimes that is where the deepest battles happen.
Not in public.
But in the quiet places where nobody sees how tired you are.
Where nobody knows how many times you have wanted to quit.
Where you keep serving even though your heart feels bruised.
Where you are tempted to believe that your life would matter more if you had someone else's opportunities.
If that is where you are, hear this carefully.
Your worth is not determined by the size of your platform.
Your salvation is not earned through the amount of work you accomplish.
And your identity before God cannot be secured by becoming indispensable to other people.
Those are burdens Jesus never asked you to carry.
Your deepest need is not to become famous for serving God.
Your deepest need is to belong to God through Jesus Christ.
And that is where this story begins moving toward something far greater than craftsmanship.
Because the tabernacle Oholiab helped construct was never intended to be the final answer to humanity's separation from God.
It belonged to a larger story.
A story of holiness.
Sin.
Sacrifice.
Mercy.
And ultimately, redemption.
But before we reach the fulfillment, we must confront something uncomfortable that happened while the tabernacle instructions were being given.
While God was speaking to Moses about the sacred dwelling place, Israel was preparing one of the most devastating acts of rebellion in its early covenant history.
The golden calf.
Exodus 32 tells us that the people became impatient during Moses' absence.
They demanded visible gods.
Aaron fashioned a golden calf.
And the people worshiped what their own hands had helped produce.
Think about the terrible contrast.
God was giving instructions for skilled hands to create objects for His appointed worship.
Meanwhile, other hands were shaping an idol.
The issue was not that one group possessed artistic ability and the other did not.
The issue was worship.
What were those hands serving?
The living God?
Or something created to take His place?
And that question reaches across the centuries.
Because idols are not always made of gold.
Sometimes they are made of approval.
Sometimes success.
Sometimes money.
Sometimes reputation.
Sometimes the desperate need to be admired.
And sometimes, painfully, even ministry can become a place where we begin seeking our own glory rather than God's.
We can become so obsessed with being seen doing something for Jesus that we slowly stop looking at Jesus Himself.
That is a frightening possibility.
And no amount of talent can protect us from it.
A person can be gifted and still be proud.
Skilled and still be spiritually careless.
Busy in religious activity and still be distant from God.
The solution is not merely to work harder.
It is to repent and return to the Lord.
The golden calf was a scandal of covenant unfaithfulness.
Yet Israel's story did not end at that moment.
Moses interceded.
God judged sin.
And the covenant narrative continued through divine mercy and renewed instruction.
Then, remarkably, the construction of the tabernacle moved forward.
Exodus 36:1–2 shows Bezalel, Oholiab, and the other skilled workers being called to perform the work God had commanded.
Do you see the movement of the story?
Sin had exposed the people's unfaithfulness.
Yet God had not abandoned His redemptive purposes.
That does not make rebellion harmless.
Grace never means sin was insignificant.
But it does reveal something astonishing about God's mercy.
Human failure did not overturn His covenant purposes.
And that prepares us to understand why the tabernacle ultimately points beyond itself.

The tabernacle was a sacred place of God's dwelling among Israel, but it also stood within a system of priesthood and sacrifice that revealed both the seriousness of sin and the necessity of approaching a holy God according to His provision.
The people needed more than a beautifully constructed sanctuary.
They needed atonement.
They needed forgiveness.
They needed a mediator.
And generations later, the Gospel of John announces something extraordinary.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
The Greek word translated “dwelt” is ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen), from a verb associated with pitching a tent or dwelling in a tabernacle.
John's language evokes the tabernacle theme of God's presence among His people.
The eternal Word became flesh.
Jesus Christ came among us.
Not as another craftsman constructing a sacred tent.
But as the Son of God who would accomplish what the earthly sanctuary and its sacrifices could never finally accomplish.
Hebrews 9 explains how Christ entered the greater and more perfect heavenly sanctuary, securing eternal redemption through His own blood.
The earthly tabernacle was part of the unfolding revelation.
Jesus is the fulfillment to whom that revelation points.
Oholiab helped construct a place associated with God's covenant presence.
Jesus Christ came as God the Son in human flesh, and through His death and resurrection He opened the way for sinners to draw near to God.
And here is where the story becomes intensely personal.
Because maybe your greatest struggle is not being overlooked.
Maybe it is being ashamed.
Maybe there are things in your past that you hope nobody discovers.
Things you said.
Things you did.
Promises you broke.
People you hurt.
Choices you wish you could undo.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to build a respectable life over the ruins of something you deeply regret.
You serve.
You smile.
You attend church.
You say the right words.
But somewhere underneath the surface, you wonder whether God could truly receive someone who has failed as badly as you have.
And this is where you must understand the difference between being useful and being redeemed.
You do not become acceptable to God by building something impressive for Him. You are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
And those who belong to Christ are created in Him for good works.
Grace comes first.
Then the transformed life follows.
You do not work your way into forgiveness.
You receive forgiveness through Christ, and then you learn to live in grateful obedience.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement disguised as salvation.
Not religious performance dressed up as holiness.
Not the exhausting attempt to make God love you by proving how valuable you are.
Jesus died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds mercy in the Savior who is able to save completely.
This is why the message of Oholiab matters so much.
It reminds us that God values faithful service.
But the larger biblical story reminds us that faithful service must never replace the Savior.
Your hands may build.
Your mind may create.
Your voice may teach.
But only Christ can save.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing you can do today is stop trying to prove that you deserve God's attention and begin responding to the grace He has revealed in His Son.
There is another detail in Oholiab's story that deserves attention.
His Hebrew name is written:
אָהֳלִיאָב — Oholiav
It is commonly understood to mean “my father's tent” or “tent of the father.”
The name contains an element associated with a tent and another associated with a father.
That is a striking name for a man involved in building the tabernacle.
But we must be careful.

Scripture does not explicitly say that Oholiab received this name prophetically because of his future work. Nor does it teach that the meaning of his name was intended as a hidden prediction of Jesus Christ.
We do not need to invent those claims to appreciate the beauty of the connection.
His name evokes a tent.
His assignment involved the sacred dwelling place.
And the larger biblical story leads us toward Jesus Christ, through whom believers are brought into fellowship with the Father.
John 14:6 records Jesus declaring that no one comes to the Father except through Him.
That is the foundation of our hope.
Not the symbolism of a craftsman's name.
Not a secret code hidden in Hebrew letters.
But the clear testimony of Scripture concerning the Son of God.
And there is another lesson here for anyone who has been entrusted with influence, knowledge, or resources.
Oholiab was not called to keep his skill to himself.
Exodus 35:34 shows that he was equipped to teach.
That means his contribution included helping other people participate in the work.
There is something deeply Christlike about serving without making yourself the center.
Not because Oholiab himself was a substitute for Christ, but because Christian service, viewed through the New Testament, should reflect the humility of our Lord.
Jesus told His disciples that greatness among them must be expressed through service.
He washed their feet.
He gave Himself for others.
And He called His followers to love one another.
So perhaps the question is not simply, “What has God given me?”
Perhaps it is also, “Whom can I strengthen with what I have received?”
Can you encourage someone who is struggling?
Can you teach a younger believer?
Can you help someone understand Scripture?
Can you give without demanding public recognition?
Can you serve faithfully even when the reward is not immediate?
Can you celebrate another person's calling without despising your own?
That last question can hurt.
Because sometimes we are not angry that God has given us nothing.
We are angry that He has given someone else something different.
And comparison can make even genuine blessings feel inadequate.
But the body of Christ is not meant to function as a competition.
First Corinthians 12 teaches that believers have different gifts and roles, yet belong to one body.
The less visible members are not therefore disposable.
Each part matters within the life of the body.
The church needs faithful teachers.
It also needs those who encourage, give, serve, organize, disciple, and show mercy.
Not every contribution will be public.
Not every sacrifice will be remembered by history.
And not every faithful believer will have a name that becomes familiar to thousands.
But there is no biblical basis for concluding that unseen obedience is meaningless.
Jesus Himself taught in Matthew 6 that the Father sees what is done in secret.
That should comfort us.
And it should also humble us.
Because God sees more than the work.
He sees the heart.
He sees whether our generosity is sincere.
He sees whether our service is motivated by love or applause.
He sees the difference between genuine devotion and spiritual performance.
And He calls us away from hypocrisy into honest fellowship with Him.
Maybe that is the word you needed today.
Not another demand to become more productive.
Not another voice telling you that you are falling behind.
But a reminder that your life is not measured by the number of people who know your name.
You can be faithful without being famous.
You can be useful without being applauded.
You can be deeply loved by God without becoming the center of attention.
And you can rest in Christ without turning every act of service into a desperate attempt to earn your worth.
But please do not misunderstand.
This is not an invitation to become passive.
Grace does not make obedience irrelevant.
It gives obedience its proper foundation.
If God has entrusted you with a gift, use it responsibly.
If you have an opportunity to serve, do so with humility.
If you have neglected a responsibility, repent.
If you have used your abilities for sinful purposes, turn away from that misuse and submit your life to Christ.
And if you have been hiding your gifts because you are afraid of being inadequate, remember that the Christian life is not built on self-sufficiency.
It is lived through dependence on the Lord.
The same God who cares about the heart also cares about what we do with the opportunities before us.
You may not be building a tabernacle.
But you may be building trust in a broken home.
You may be helping rebuild a relationship damaged by years of bitterness.
You may be teaching a child to pray.
You may be helping a struggling believer understand the Gospel.
You may be supporting the spread of sound biblical teaching.
You may be quietly serving in ways that no social media platform will ever celebrate.
Do not despise those things merely because they are ordinary.
And do not turn them into a reason for pride.
Offer them to the Lord.
Because the ultimate purpose of Christian service is not to make our names great.
It is to glorify the name of Jesus Christ.
That is also why the mission of Gospel Warrior matters to us.
We do not want people merely to admire powerful Christian words for a few seconds and then continue unchanged.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To examine the Scriptures.
To repent where repentance is needed.
To receive the grace of Jesus Christ.
To grow in sound doctrine.
To find encouragement in difficult seasons.
And to become faithful disciples who are able to strengthen others.
That is why we continue developing biblical articles, devotionals, books, and discipleship resources.
We believe biblical nourishment should reach people who are hungry for truth, including those who may not have the resources to purchase Christian study materials.
But sustaining and expanding this work requires time, effort, resources, and people willing to participate.
And here is where Oholiab's story offers a practical challenge.
God's work among His people involved different contributions.
Some were called to craftsmanship.
Others supplied materials.
Others taught.
The tabernacle account shows people participating in the work according to the instructions God had given.
Today, Christians likewise have opportunities to participate in Gospel-centered ministry through prayer, encouragement, service, generosity, and sharing biblical truth.
And not because giving money to Gospel Warrior is a biblical requirement.
It is not.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be a matter of the heart, not something extracted through pressure or compulsion.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Those products are not the reason to support the Gospel.
They are simply one way we want to express appreciation to those who choose to stand with this ministry.
You can still be part of this mission.
Pray for the ministry.
Share biblical truth.
Encourage someone who is losing hope.
Help another believer understand the Scriptures.
A thoughtful share may introduce this passage to someone who has never heard of Oholiab.
Someone who has been serving quietly for years.
Someone who has begun believing that their life does not matter.
Someone who is exhausted from comparing themselves with others.
Someone who needs to remember that Christ is more than enough.
You do not know who might be reading silently.
The friend who never comments.
The family member who has drifted from church.
The person who appears successful but is privately overwhelmed by shame.
The believer who still prays but has almost lost the courage to hope.
Sharing an article cannot guarantee anyone's conversion or healing.
Only God can bring spiritual life.
But faithful words of Scripture can become part of the witness through which someone hears the truth.
Not to chase numbers.
Not to collect attention.
But because the Gospel is worth making known.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them—not to expose their struggle, but to encourage them personally.
Perhaps write a simple message:
Sometimes people do not need another public compliment.
They need to know someone sees the weight they have been carrying.
And if this article spoke to something you have been struggling with, I want to invite you to do something more personal.
Not a polished religious performance.
Not something designed to impress strangers.
Just an honest response.
You do not have to reveal private details or confess sensitive matters publicly.
God knows what you are carrying.
And the Christian community should be a place where people can encourage one another toward Christ rather than compete over appearances.
For the days when serving becomes exhausting.
For the days when your efforts seem forgotten.
For the days when you need to remember that your identity rests in Christ, not in the recognition of people.
And invite your family, your friends, those who are struggling in faith, those who are spiritually indifferent, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to explore the Scriptures with us.
Not everyone who encounters a Christian message will agree with it.
But everyone deserves to hear the Gospel presented faithfully, without distortion or manipulation.
And perhaps that is the greatest responsibility we carry.
Not to make the message more sensational than Scripture.
Not to invent hidden meanings where God has not revealed them.
Not to promise earthly rewards the Bible never guarantees.
But to handle God's Word carefully and point people to the Savior it reveals.
Because the most unforgettable part of Oholiab's story is not that he became famous.
He did not.
Even today, many believers know the name of Bezalel but struggle to remember Oholiab.
Yet his name remains in the biblical record.
His work mattered within the construction of the tabernacle.
And the tabernacle itself belonged to the unfolding story that finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
That is enough to make us reconsider what greatness really means.
You may spend your life doing work that history never records.
You may help people who eventually forget your name.
And none of those things automatically makes you righteous before God.
Only Christ can reconcile you to the Father.
But when you belong to Jesus, you are free to serve without making human recognition your ultimate reward.
You no longer need to turn every assignment into a stage.
You no longer need to see another person's success as a threat.
You no longer need to confuse being overlooked by people with being abandoned by God.
You can serve faithfully.
You can repent when pride rises.
You can rest when you are weary.
You can rejoice when someone else is honored.
And you can remember that the Lord sees what people do not.
There is a reason this matters beyond the story of one ancient craftsman.
One day, every earthly title will lose its power to impress.
Every platform will become irrelevant.
Every applause-filled moment will fade.
And what will matter is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
Not whether we were impressive enough.
Not whether our achievements were extraordinary enough.
But whether we trusted the Savior who died and rose again, and whether our lives bore the fruit of that faith.
The Gospel does not promise that faithful Christians will always be recognized in this life.
It promises something better.
In Christ, we have forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the hope of eternal life.
And because of that grace, even ordinary service can be offered with extraordinary gratitude.
So if you are the person working quietly while everyone else receives attention, do not lose heart.
If you are the person who has been comparing your gifts with someone else's, surrender that burden to Christ.
If you are the person who has been hiding behind religious activity while your heart is far from God, repent and return to Him.
And if you are the person who believes your past has made you too stained to be received by Jesus, remember what the Gospel actually announces.
Christ came to save sinners.
The cross reveals the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection declares the victory of our Savior.
And grace calls us not merely to feel better about ourselves, but to turn from sin and live as people made new in Him.
That is the journey from scandal to grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not excusing rebellion.
Not hiding brokenness beneath beautiful religious language.
But bringing our guilt, our pride, our wounds, and our failures into the light of the Gospel.
And discovering that Jesus Christ is able to forgive, redeem, and transform those who come to Him in faith.
Oholiab's hands helped build a sanctuary.
But the hands of Jesus Christ were pierced for sinners.
Oholiab served within the covenant worship of ancient Israel.
But Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant.
Oholiab participated in constructing a dwelling place made with human hands.
But through Christ, God's people are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit, as Ephesians 2:22 teaches.
That is where our eyes must finally rest.
Not on the craftsman.
Not on the craftsmanship.
Not even on the tabernacle.
But on Jesus.
The One greater than every earthly sanctuary.
The One who brings sinners near to God.
The One who does not merely give us something meaningful to do, but gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And perhaps tonight, you do not need a bigger platform.
Perhaps you need a quieter heart.
A heart that can say:
Lord, if You want me to serve where nobody applauds, teach me to be faithful.
If You want me to help someone else succeed, teach me to rejoice.
If I have been serving for recognition, forgive me.
If I have buried what You entrusted to me, help me repent and act.
If I have mistaken my usefulness for my worth, bring me back to the cross.
And if I have forgotten that everything begins and ends with Jesus, turn my eyes toward Him again.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be to live and die without the world remembering your name.
The greatest tragedy would be to spend your life chasing recognition while neglecting the Savior who alone can give you life.
Oholiab reminds us that a person can be little known and still have a meaningful place in God's work.
Jesus reminds us that our greatest hope is not found in the work of our hands, but in His finished work.
And when that truth finally settles into your soul, something begins to change.
You can stop fighting for the spotlight.
You can stop resenting the gifts of others.
You can stop pretending to be stronger than you are.
You can begin serving from gratitude rather than insecurity.
You can offer your gifts without worshiping them.
And you can trust that the God who knows every name in His Book also knows the hearts of those who belong to His Son.
So remember Oholiab.
Remember the forgotten craftsman.
Remember the sacred work.
Remember the danger of idolatry.
Remember the mercy of God.
But above all, remember Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the applause of this world will fall silent.
And the question will never have been how many people remembered your name.
The question is whether your name was known by the Savior you were called to follow.
